dimensions.name: Scope
dimensions.summary: The size and time-horizon of the work the PM owns end-to-end

dimensions.name: Ambiguity tolerance
dimensions.summary: Comfort and competence when the goal isn't pre-defined

dimensions.name: Influence
dimensions.summary: Ability to move people who don't report to the PM

dimensions.name: Judgment
dimensions.summary: Quality of decisions made under incomplete information

dimensions.name: Craft
dimensions.summary: Depth of skill in the trade itself (writing, research, data, AI literacy)

levels.title: APM / Associate PM
levels.anchor: Owns small slices; needs ambient direction

levels.title: PM
levels.anchor: Owns features that ship in one sprint; informed by clear product direction

levels.title: Senior PM
levels.anchor: Owns multi-sprint initiatives; sets product direction for a small surface

levels.title: Staff PM
levels.anchor: Owns product lines or platform direction; influences strategy at the org level

levels.title: Principal PM
levels.anchor: Owns bets that define the next 12-18 months; sets craft standards for the function

questions.text: Largest decision you owned end-to-end in your most recent quarter.
options: A feature flag, a copy change, or a single UI component.
A feature that shipped in one sprint, end-to-end.
A multi-team initiative that spanned the whole quarter.
A product line or platform direction that affected multiple teams.
A bet that defines where the business is going in the next 12-18 months.

questions.text: Time horizon of your typical commitments.
options: The current sprint. Two weeks out, at most.
This quarter. You think about what ships in the next three months.
Two or three quarters out. You carry strategy across planning seasons.
Six to twelve months out. You anchor the roadmap conversation for your area.
Twelve to eighteen months out. Your conviction shapes the company's long-range bets.

questions.text: Number of teams affected by your typical work.
options: Your own team, or a small pod. One surface, minimal coordination.
One or two teams. You coordinate occasionally with adjacent functions.
Three or more teams. You own the cross-team outcome.
An entire org area. Multiple squads, one direction.
The whole product org. Your work sets the direction others orient around.

questions.text: Customer segment scope (a feature, a segment, or the whole market).
options: One user flow or a narrow feature edge case.
A coherent feature set that one user persona cares about.
A customer segment or a recognized product surface.
Multiple segments, or a platform layer all customers depend on.
The market itself. Your work shapes how the company positions against competitors.

questions.text: Strategic-to-tactical mix in your week.
options: Mostly tactical. Tickets, standups, and responding to questions.
About 80% tactical, 20% looking ahead. You own the near-term roadmap.
Roughly half and half. You're in planning conversations as often as in execution.
More strategy than execution. You spend your week unblocking others more than shipping personally.
Primarily strategic. Your week is shaped by where the org needs direction, not by the sprint board.

questions.text: Org-level visibility of your work (who reviews it).
options: Your direct manager reviews your work before it ships.
Your team lead, with occasional skip-level review of key artifacts.
A director or VP reviews your roadmap before it goes to the broader team.
Senior leadership has input into your area. C-level is occasionally in the loop.
You present to execs and board-level stakeholders. Your work sets the reference point others are measured against.

questions.text: What you do when the goal isn't pre-defined.
options: You wait for your manager to clarify the goal before starting.
You draft a rough problem statement and get your manager's sign-off before moving.
You define the goal yourself, write it up, and socialize it until stakeholders align.
You set the problem definition for a large surface and make it the team's north star across multiple squads.
You define the problem space others work within. When the org doesn't know what it's optimizing for, that's your question to answer.

questions.text: Default response when data is missing.
options: You wait for data. You feel blocked making calls without numbers.
You make the call but hedge heavily and flag the gap upward.
You state your confidence level, name the assumption you're making, decide, and schedule a review.
You apply a reversibility test, sequence the decision, and commission the missing data in parallel.
You structure the sequence of bets so the easiest ones generate the data the harder ones need.

questions.text: How you handle conflicting requirements between two senior stakeholders.
options: You escalate to your manager. Not sure how to proceed without their call.
You try to find a middle path that satisfies both. It often ends up serving neither.
You write a one-pager surfacing the tradeoffs and ask the stakeholders to decide together.
You mediate the conflict directly. It rarely needs to escalate; you anchor on the shared goal.
You mostly prevent these conflicts. The strategy is clear enough upstream that they rarely reach the team.

questions.text: Reaction time to a leadership pivot.
options: You need significant re-explanation before the team can move. The disruption is visible.
It takes a sprint or two to reorient. The team can tell there was a direction change.
Within a week, you have a revised plan that integrates the pivot. The team is moving again.
You had a contingency sketch ready. The team barely notices the turn.
You helped shape the pivot. Your read of the market fed the leadership conversation. The team is already moving before the announcement.

questions.text: Comfort with shipping a product you're not 100% sure about.
options: You wait for more research or more sign-offs before shipping with meaningful uncertainty.
You ship when directed to, but flag the uncertainty upward. You don't fully own the risk.
You set kill criteria and a rollback plan before shipping. Success metrics are defined up front.
You distinguish reversible from irreversible risk, ship fast on Type-2 decisions, and explain the logic to the team.
You define what 'good enough to ship' means for the current product stage. Teams use your framework.

questions.text: How you frame 'I don't know' out loud.
options: You avoid saying it directly. You stay quiet or deflect when you don't have the answer.
You say it, but it sounds apologetic and you don't follow it with structure.
You say 'I don't know yet' and follow it with what you're doing to find out, and by when.
You separate what can be found out from what has to be decided under uncertainty, and use that to frame the next step.
You make it safe for everyone to say what they don't know. Decision logs and pre-mortems are team norms because of you.

questions.text: How you handle disagreement with engineering leadership.
options: You escalate to your manager. You're not confident taking disagreements directly to engineering leadership.
You raise your concern once. If it doesn't land, you defer and move on.
You make the case directly: data, reasoning, and a specific ask. You know when the argument is settled.
Engineering leads treat your perspective as input before finalizing direction. Disagreements rarely escalate; trust does the work.
Engineering leadership seeks your read proactively. When you push back, it shapes the outcome.

questions.text: How exec stakeholders engage with your work (and at what cadence).
options: Execs don't engage with your work directly. Your manager relays context when it matters.
An exec occasionally shows up to a review. It's not a regular pattern.
A director or VP reviews your roadmap quarterly and provides input before it goes to the broader team.
You have a standing exec forum for your area. C-level is in the loop on material decisions.
You present to C-level and board-level stakeholders on a regular cadence. Your work anchors what others bring to those rooms.

questions.text: Cross-functional pull (does design, GTM, and data come to you proactively).
options: Cross-functional partners wait for you to kick things off. They don't seek your input unless you ask.
An occasional proactive reach from one partner, usually for a handoff, not a planning conversation.
Design and engineering come to you proactively on direction. GTM occasionally loops you in early.
Multiple functions treat you as the first call on strategic decisions. You're in their planning cadences without needing to push.
Functions use your frame before starting their own planning. Your judgment is load-bearing across the org.

questions.text: Mentorship reach (how many PMs you have ongoing coaching relationships with).
options: None yet. You're still building the skills you'd coach others on.
One informal relationship — someone who reaches out occasionally for advice.
One or two ongoing relationships with more junior PMs. Regular check-ins, structured feedback, or shared artifacts.
Three or more active coaching relationships. You've seen PMs you coached get promoted.
You set the craft standard for the PM function. You coach the coaches and your development model shapes how junior PMs are grown in your org.

questions.text: External visibility (talks, writing, hiring panels).
options: No external footprint. Your work is fully internal.
One or two external moments — a conference talk, a post that traveled outside the company. Not a deliberate pattern.
You've spoken at one or two external venues, published publicly, or served on hiring advisory panels. People outside your company know your name.
Recognized by PM peers outside your company. Invited to podcast appearances, external events, or advisory roles on a recurring basis.
A reference point in the field. Your writing, talks, or frameworks are cited by others. You shape how PMs outside your company think about craft.

questions.text: How you frame proposals (which audience do you build for).
options: You write for your manager. The proposal's job is to get sign-off from one person.
You write for your immediate team and stakeholders. Your engineer and designer can follow the reasoning.
You write for multiple audiences in one doc. Engineering leads and business stakeholders each get the signal they need from the same artifact.
You write for senior leaders who don't have the product context. Strategic linkage is explicit; a VP can share it upward without translation.
Your proposals don't need translation at any level. You write at company scope by default; functional teams use your framing as their working context.

questions.text: How you make trade-offs under time pressure.
options: You default to the safe option or delay the call. Picking wrong feels riskier than not deciding.
You escalate to your manager before moving. A hard call needs sign-off before you commit.
You apply the reversibility test: fast on Type-2 decisions, slower on Type-1. You decide and log the reasoning.
Your team has a shared framework for categorizing decisions. When pressure hits, the call usually doesn't need you in the room.
The upstream strategy is clear enough that genuine trade-off calls are rare. When they do come, the framework is already there.

questions.text: Calibration on your bets (do you track confidence at the time of decision).
options: You don't formally track confidence. You learn by watching what worked.
You have a rough memory of how confident you were, but nothing written down.
You log key decisions and your confidence level when you make them. You review the log quarterly and look for patterns.
Every significant bet has defined kill criteria before it launches. You revisit the criteria at each major milestone.
Your decision log is a team artifact. Others calibrate their judgment against yours over time; the log is a reference, not a personal exercise.

questions.text: How you handle a failed launch.
options: You focus on what went wrong in the build or the spec. Failure is a technical problem to fix.
You run a retrospective, document the learnings, and move on. The team's culture around failure is whatever it was before.
You separate the decision from the outcome. You document what you knew, what you assumed, and where the reasoning broke down, and share it openly.
The launch review process is designed for failure to be visible and safe to name. The post-mortem template exists before the launch does.
Kill criteria are defined before the bet launches. When you stop something, the reasoning is already documented and the team expected the possibility.

questions.text: Reaction to a clear signal that disconfirms your strategy.
options: You surface it to your manager. You're not sure if it changes the direction; someone senior should weigh in.
You note it but attribute it to timing or execution. The strategy probably still holds.
You revisit the key assumptions explicitly. You document what the signal means for the bet and decide whether to hold, adjust, or stop.
You convene the right people within days. You don't let the signal age. The team re-examines the bet with the new data in the room.
You pre-defined how to weight this class of signal before the bet launched. The stop criteria are already documented; the signal triggers the review process.

questions.text: Stop-doing list quality (what you cut last quarter and why).
options: You don't have a stop-doing list. Your work is what gets assigned to you.
Some things got deprioritized last quarter, but it was mostly sprint constraints, not a deliberate call.
You cut at least one initiative last quarter with a rationale you could articulate to stakeholders. The team knew it was a decision, not just a reprioritization.
Your stop-doing list is deliberate and visible. You can name what you killed and why, in terms of strategy, not capacity.
Your cuts are the most important decisions you make each quarter. When you stop something, the org reads it. The reasoning is public and shapes how others prioritize.

questions.text: Speed-vs-quality discernment (which call was wrong in your last 90 days).
options: You can't easily name a specific instance where you explicitly traded speed for quality or vice versa.
You know in retrospect you either moved too slow or shipped something too rough, but you're not sure which pattern is the problem.
You can name a specific call from the last 90 days where you made an explicit speed-vs-quality tradeoff, and you know whether the call was right.
Your team has a shared frame for which calls are 'go fast' vs 'slow down and get it right.' You built the model; they use it.
Your team's default calibration on speed vs quality is part of how you run the product. New team members learn the frame from how you model it, not from a document.

questions.text: Quality of your written artifacts (specs, decision docs).
options: You write specs when asked. Format varies; you're still learning what belongs in one.
You follow a template and cover the required sections. The doc works for your immediate team.
Your specs are problem-first, have explicit success criteria and non-goals, and are short enough to be read. Stakeholders rarely ask what a doc is trying to accomplish.
Your artifacts are the reference point other teams use for their own planning. You rarely have to explain a document you wrote.
Your authoring discipline shapes how the team writes. When someone asks how to structure a decision doc, they use yours as the example.

questions.text: Customer-research depth (frequency and shape).
options: You read support tickets and aggregate feedback surveys. You haven't run your own customer interviews recently.
You run interviews for major features. You tend to ask customers what they want, not what they've done.
You run story-based interviews on a regular cadence — past behavior, not hypotheticals. Findings feed into your next planning cycle.
Discovery is a team cadence, not just your personal practice. Engineers and designers are in the room. You synthesize and bring findings into roadmap decisions.
Your discovery process is what the team uses. How you interview and synthesize is how the org does it. Your methods are the default, not just your own habit.

questions.text: Data fluency (what you can run yourself vs ask for).
options: You read dashboards and ask the data team for queries. You can't analyze data independently.
You can filter and pivot dashboards. You know which metric to look at; the data team builds the analysis you need.
You write basic SQL, build cohort cuts, and set up experiments with reasonable success criteria. You don't need the data team to walk you through the setup.
You and the data team co-author experiments. You frame hypotheses clearly, understand confound risk, and can push back on a misread A/B result.
Your data fluency sets the team's analytical standard. You're the PM others come to for experiment design, and your metric definitions are the ones the team runs on.

questions.text: Design-quality literacy (can you red-line a design).
options: You can tell when something looks off, but you can't name what's wrong or say how to fix it.
You give flow-level feedback: missing states, confusing labels, wrong behavior. Not craft-level feedback.
You review designs against the user need and give feedback a designer can act on. You hold back from specifying pixels; you name the problem, not the solution.
Your design reviews raise the quality bar. Designers find your feedback specific and directionally useful. You prototype quickly when you need to communicate intent.
Product coherence at the system level is partly your responsibility. You can name what erodes it and say no when something ships that doesn't fit. Designers treat your taste as a useful signal.

questions.text: Engineering-system literacy (can you read a service map).
options: You know what the product does but not how the systems under it work.
You know the rough architecture of your area and can discuss technical trade-offs in general terms.
You can read a service diagram, ask useful questions about latency and failure modes, and size build costs on roadmap items without needing engineering to do it for you.
Engineers include you in architecture discussions where the decision affects the product. You catch cross-system implications before they become scope creep.
You've shipped production features or built real prototypes against system constraints. Engineers treat you as a technical peer on product-adjacent decisions.

questions.text: AI and eval literacy (do you ship AI features with an eval set).
options: You use AI as a consumer. You haven't shipped an AI feature or written an eval.
You've shipped AI features but relied on spot checks and vibe testing to gauge quality. Evals aren't yet part of how you ship.
You can read traces, identify failure modes, and contribute to defining eval criteria. You don't ship AI features on vibe alone.
Your team has an eval suite that exists before each AI launch. You built the failure-mode taxonomy from real traces, and the team updates it as the model changes.
Your eval methodology is the standard the org uses. Other teams reference how you built yours. The pass-rate trend on your AI features is a documented artifact reviewed at every major milestone.
